project: Human Atlas — Lymphoid System and Immunity

subject.courseChapterTitle: Chapter 22 — The Lymphoid System and Immunity

immunity.role: Main Chapter 22 lymphoid physiology and immunity lecture; immune cell mechanisms, organs, innate/adaptive defense, antibodies and immunologic memory.

anatomy.role: Complementary anatomy/model identification, drainage, lymph-node histology, thymus, spleen, tonsils, MALT and fat absorption.

studyGuide.role: Instructor-supplied explicit exam objectives, without implying that unlisted slide material is excluded.

overview: The new subject must bridge physical lymph transport, organ structure and cellular immunity rather than treating them as disconnected topics. Same educational register and reusable eight-tab interface as Digestive.

courseCoverage.prompt: What are the functions of the lymphatic system?
courseCoverage.keyConcept: Three interconnected functions: fluid recovery, immune surveillance, dietary lipid transport
courseCoverage.notes: Include lecture-specific wording: defense / lymphocyte production / filtration and monitoring.

courseCoverage.prompt: How do lymphatic capillaries differ from blood capillaries? Why does lymph only enter, but not exit lymph capillaries?
courseCoverage.keyConcept: Blind-ended lymphatic capillaries vs blood capillaries; overlapping endothelial entry flaps

courseCoverage.prompt: Why do lymphatic vessels have valves?
courseCoverage.keyConcept: One-way valves and mechanisms propelling low-pressure lymph

courseCoverage.prompt: What is lymph?
courseCoverage.keyConcept: Define plasma, interstitial fluid and lymph by compartment

courseCoverage.prompt: What are the 3 lymphatic organs? What makes a lymphatic organ different from a lymphatic tissue?
courseCoverage.keyConcept: Three encapsulated lymphoid organs in course classification vs nonencapsulated tissue
courseCoverage.notes: The lecture’s three: lymph nodes, thymus, spleen. Clarify broader primary/secondary lymphoid organ classification separately.

courseCoverage.prompt: What are the 2 major ducts and from where in the body do they collect lymph from?
courseCoverage.keyConcept: Right lymphatic duct vs thoracic duct territories

courseCoverage.prompt: What 3 trunks deliver lymph to the right lymphatic duct?  What 6 trunks deliver lymph to the thoracic duct (or cisterna chyli)?
courseCoverage.keyConcept: Three trunks for right duct; six inputs listed for thoracic duct/cisterna chyli
courseCoverage.notes: Right: jugular, subclavian, bronchomediastinal. Left: those three plus intestinal and right/left lumbar; distinguish direct thoracic duct vs cisterna chyli entry.

courseCoverage.prompt: Where do the thoracic and right lymphatic duct deliver lymph to the venous system (what veins)?
courseCoverage.keyConcept: Venous returns at left and right jugulosubclavian venous angles
courseCoverage.notes: Lecture calls these the left and right subclavian veins; include anatomical confluences in Deep Dive.

courseCoverage.prompt: What are the 3 classes of lymphocytes? Which have specific defenses? What is their mode of defense? Which have nonspecific defense?
courseCoverage.keyConcept: T, B and NK lymphocytes; adaptive versus innate mechanisms

courseCoverage.prompt: Discuss the derivation and distribution of lymphocytes (where lymphopoeisis takes place): Where do T-cells develop? What hormone (presence of) stimulates B-cell differentiation. What if it is not present?
courseCoverage.keyConcept: Lymphopoiesis and T/B-cell developmental compartments; unresolved hormone wording
courseCoverage.notes: The study guide asks which hormone stimulates B-cell differentiation, but supplied slides identify thymosins with T-cell development. Flag to clarify with instructor.

courseCoverage.prompt: What happens in the germinal center?
courseCoverage.keyConcept: Germinal centers and proliferating lymphocytes

courseCoverage.prompt: What is the function of lymph nodes? Discuss the movement of lymph through them and how pathogens are attacked and destroyed.
courseCoverage.keyConcept: Lymph-node filtration and spatial pathway through sinuses; B-cell cortex and T-cell paracortex
courseCoverage.notes: Do not interpret cortex → paracortex as lymph physically passing through a succession of B cells and T cells.

courseCoverage.prompt: What is the function of the thymus? What cells help to maintain the blood-thymus barrier? What is function of blood-thymus barrier?  What is involution?
courseCoverage.keyConcept: Thymus, blood-thymus barrier, reticular epithelial cells, involution

courseCoverage.prompt: What are the functions of the spleen?  Understand the pathway of blood flow through the spleen and how pathogens are attacked.
courseCoverage.keyConcept: Spleen: red/white pulp, blood flow, immune function, RBC clearance

courseCoverage.prompt: What are the 7 non-specific defenses and how do they work?
courseCoverage.keyConcept: Exactly seven instructor-listed nonspecific defenses and their mechanisms

courseCoverage.prompt: How do NK cells kill an abnormal cell?
courseCoverage.keyConcept: Natural killer recognition and perforin/granzyme-mediated cytotoxicity
courseCoverage.notes: Granzyme mechanism is a scientifically relevant extension; slide highlights perforin and lysis.

courseCoverage.prompt: What is inflammation and what are the cardinal signs and symptoms of inflammation?
courseCoverage.keyConcept: Inflammation, classic four signs and fever
courseCoverage.notes: Instructor lists tumor, rubor, calor, “dolar”; standard Latin spelling is dolor.

courseCoverage.prompt: What are the types of immunity?
courseCoverage.keyConcept: Innate vs adaptive; active vs passive, natural vs induced acquired immunity
courseCoverage.notes: Keep distinct axes: innate/adaptive and active/passive; do not repeat ambiguous hierarchy from slide 36 uncritically.

courseCoverage.prompt: Contrast B-cell and T-cells. Compare antibody mediated immunity and cell mediated immunity (understand steps of antigen presentation and antibody production).
courseCoverage.keyConcept: Cell-mediated vs humoral immunity, helper T-cell signaling and antibody production

courseCoverage.prompt: Understand the differences in Class I MHCs and Class II MHCS and what happens when those are recognized by other cells.
courseCoverage.keyConcept: MHC class I vs class II: location, source of antigen, responding CD8/CD4 cells

courseCoverage.prompt: Which class of MHC tells the body that a cell is infected or abnormal? What is the fate of that cell?
courseCoverage.keyConcept: MHC I peptide recognition by cytotoxic T cells and target-cell fate
courseCoverage.notes: MHC I is normally expressed, not merely an infection-exclusive red flag.

courseCoverage.prompt: Which class of MHC tells the body that an antigen is dangerous and it needs to be destroyed? What is produced to destroy the antigen?
courseCoverage.keyConcept: MHC II presentation to helper T cells and downstream immune activation

courseCoverage.prompt: What type of cell activates B cells? What 2 types of cells are produced after activation and division? What do B-cells differentiate into before they can produce antibodies?
courseCoverage.keyConcept: Activated helper T cells, B-cell proliferation, plasma cells and memory B cells

courseCoverage.prompt: What is an antigen determinant site?
courseCoverage.keyConcept: Antigenic determinant = epitope, binding of antibody variable regions

courseCoverage.prompt: What are the types of antibodies and their major function?
courseCoverage.keyConcept: Immunoglobulin classes IgG, IgM, IgA, IgE, IgD and course functions

courseCoverage.prompt: What is opsonization? What is neutralization?
courseCoverage.keyConcept: Opsonization vs neutralization and other antibody effector actions

courseCoverage.prompt: What is antibody titer? Contrast primary vs. secondary response
courseCoverage.keyConcept: Antibody titer and primary vs secondary responses (time and magnitude)

courseCoverage.prompt: What is appendicitis? What is AIDS? What happens during an autoimmune disorder (disease)?
courseCoverage.keyConcept: Appendicitis, HIV/AIDS, autoimmune disorders and given examples
courseCoverage.notes: Avoid oversimplified claims about all HIV infections or always-fatal common colds.

general-overview.label: General Overview
general-overview.style: Welcoming, readable, concise, pedagogically progressive. Two brief opening paragraphs; eight short titled sections; bullets only for a route, list, or contrast. No encyclopedic dump.
general-overview.introConcept: The body constantly exchanges fluid with its tissues and is constantly exposed to molecules that may be harmless or dangerous. The lymphoid system recovers excess fluid, examines it for threats, and maintains immune cells that can react appropriately.

sections.title: Three Jobs, One System
sections.purpose: Establish tissue-fluid recovery, immune surveillance/defense, and absorption of dietary fats; mention lymphocyte production. Avoid confusing an anatomical system with the totality of immune responses.

sections.title: From Blood Plasma to Interstitial Fluid to Lymph
sections.purpose: Explain the same water-containing extracellular fluid by compartment; simple capillary/interstitial/lymphatic path.

sections.title: The One-Way Route Back to Blood
sections.purpose: Flow from lymphatic capillaries to collecting vessels, nodes, trunks, ducts and venous circulation; explain valves and unequal drainage territories.

sections.title: Three Major Lymphocyte Classes
sections.purpose: Introduce B cells, T cells and NK cells; differentiate adaptive specificity from innate surveillance.

sections.title: Where Immune Cells Develop and Meet
sections.purpose: Lymph nodes vs thymus vs spleen; add marrow and distributed mucosal lymphoid tissue, distinguishing function and filter target.

sections.title: The Immediate Defenses
sections.purpose: Organize skin/barriers, phagocytes, NK cells, interferons, complement, inflammation and fever without yet explaining each cascade.

sections.title: Specific Recognition and Immune Memory
sections.purpose: Introduce antigen recognition, helper vs cytotoxic responses, antibodies, and why secondary exposure can be faster.

sections.title: What You Should Be Able to Identify
sections.purpose: Distinguish lymph node regions, duct territories, thymus, spleen, tonsils and MALT; prepare for lecture models and Gallery.

deep-dive.label: Deep Dive
deep-dive.style: Same educational voice as Digestive Deep Dive: explanatory prose, bold anatomical terms, clear mechanisms and physical pathways, appropriate tables, source-slide references by section. Preserve course terminology and place meaningful scientific qualifications immediately beside simplified lecture claims.
deep-dive.introConcept: An instructor-aligned reference to the Chapter 22 study guide, expanded with the model/anatomy presentation and selected scientific context.

sections.title: Functions, Fluid Compartments, and Basic Terminology
sections.purpose: Explain roles of lymphoid system; interstitial hydrostatic/oncotic driving forces, fluid homeostasis, edema, plasma vs tissue fluid vs lymph.

sections.title: Lymphatic Capillaries and One-Way Entry
sections.purpose: Blind ends, overlapping endothelial flaps, anchoring filaments, discontinuous basal lamina, size comparison with blood capillaries; pathogen transport caveat.

sections.title: Collecting Vessels, Valves, and Lymph Propulsion
sections.purpose: Smooth muscle, skeletal muscle compression, respiratory changes, vessel valves and low-pressure transport; no central heart-like pump.

sections.title: Lymphatic Trunks, Ducts, and Drainage Territories
sections.purpose: Detail 3 right trunks, 6 source-listed left/inferior contributors, cisterna chyli, thoracic and right lymphatic ducts and venous angles; include labelled flow chart.

sections.title: Lymphoid Organs, Tissues, and Primary vs Secondary Sites
sections.purpose: Three course-defined encapsulated organs plus bone marrow and unencapsulated tissues; distinguish functional primary/secondary classifications.

sections.title: Lymph Node Microanatomy and Lymph Flow
sections.purpose: Capsule, trabeculae, hilum; afferent vs efferent; subcapsular/trabecular/medullary sinuses; cortical B follicles, T paracortex, medullary cords, macrophages, APCs, germinal centers.

sections.title: Lymphopoiesis and the Three Lymphocyte Lineages
sections.purpose: Hematopoietic origin, bone marrow, thymus, circulating lymphocytes, functional distinctions of B/T/NK; flag unresolved hormone question.

sections.title: Thymus: Architecture, T-Cell Maturation, and Involution
sections.purpose: Two lobes/lobules, cortex/medulla, epithelial reticular cells, blood-thymus barrier, thymosin terminology, age-related involution; thymocyte selection as clearly identified extension.

sections.title: Spleen: Blood Filtration and Red/White Pulp
sections.purpose: Upper-left abdominal anatomy, diaphragmatic/visceral surfaces and hilum; arterial flow, white pulp immune recognition, red pulp macrophages, RBC turnover, trauma and splenectomy.

sections.title: Tonsils, MALT, Peyer’s Patches, and Appendix
sections.purpose: Tonsil positions, Waldeyer’s ring, follicle/germinal center; GALT/BALT/NALT/MALT; local mucosal protection. Avoid overclaiming exact number of lingual tonsils.

sections.title: Seven Nonspecific Defenses and Their Functions
sections.purpose: Use exact instructor list: physical barriers, phagocytes, immunological surveillance, interferons, complement, inflammation, fever. Contrast innate rapid responses with adaptive specificity.

sections.title: Phagocytes, Natural Killer Cells, and Immunological Surveillance
sections.purpose: Neutrophils and macrophages, recognition/engulfment; NK targets, perforin/granzyme response, cancer escape as contextual example.

sections.title: Interferons, Cytokines, Complement, and the MAC
sections.purpose: Antiviral signaling, complement classical pathway from lecture; opsonization, chemotaxis/inflammation, C5b–9 MAC; distinguish complement from antibody itself.

sections.title: Inflammation and Fever
sections.purpose: Tissue injury, mast-cell/histamine effects, vasodilation, permeability, leukocyte recruitment, clotting/repair; rubor/calor/tumor/dolor, hypothalamic pyrogen response.

sections.title: Adaptive Immunity: Specificity, Memory, Tolerance, and Active/Passive Forms
sections.purpose: Specificity/versatility/memory/tolerance; adaptive vs innate; active/passive natural/artificial; B-cell humoral vs T-cell cell-mediated response.

sections.title: MHC Class I and Cytotoxic T-Cell Responses
sections.purpose: Peptides from intracellular proteins displayed by most nucleated cells; CD8+ recognition, activation, effector and memory, killing via perforin/granzyme/apoptosis.

sections.title: MHC Class II, Helper T Cells, and B-Cell Activation
sections.purpose: Professional APCs and extracellular antigen processing; CD4+ recognition, cytokine help, B-cell activation, plasma vs memory differentiation.

sections.title: Antigens, Antibody Structure, Immunoglobulin Classes, and Effector Mechanisms
sections.purpose: Epitopes, paratopes; heavy/light chain; IgG/IgM/IgA/IgE/IgD; neutralization, agglutination, opsonization, complement, pathogen adhesion.

sections.title: Primary/Secondary Responses and Clinical Connections
sections.purpose: Titer curves, IgM/IgG response patterns and memory cells; appendicitis, HIV/AIDS and autoimmunity with scientifically careful qualifications. End with an integrated flow summary.

how-it-connects.label: How It Connects
how-it-connects.style: A continuous causal narrative, like Digestive’s Journey of Digestion. Few lists. Starting problem, physical processes, cell decisions, immunological outcomes, final synthesis. Never just paste the Deep Dive headings into the story.
how-it-connects.workingTitle: From a Scrape to Immune Memory
how-it-connects.introConcept: Follow a minor skin injury, the local innate response, the journey of fluid and antigen through lymphatic vessels, the encounters inside a lymph node, and the development of antigen-specific defenses and memory.

sections.title: 1. The Hidden Problem: Tissues Are Not Sealed
sections.purpose: Start with a scrape and ordinary capillary filtration; microbes and molecules at the tissue boundary; why a transport and defense network is needed.

sections.title: 2. The First Response: Barriers, Phagocytes, and Signals
sections.purpose: An epithelial breach, immediate innate defenses, inflammation and chemical communication; no assumption that every injury causes infection.

sections.title: 3. Interstitial Fluid Finds a One-Way Exit
sections.purpose: Excess tissue fluid enters initial lymphatic capillaries; explain the mechanical flaps and valves, differentiate lymph from tissue fluid.

sections.title: 4. The Lymph Node: A Meeting Place, Not Just a Filter
sections.purpose: Regional afferent lymph brings antigens/APCs; capture in sinuses and encounter between rare antigen-specific lymphocytes.

sections.title: 5. The Two Kinds of Recognition
sections.purpose: Innate recognition versus T-cell recognition of presented peptides; B-cell receptor interaction with antigen; introduce MHC I/II where relevant.

sections.title: 6. Helper T Cells Coordinate; Cytotoxic T Cells Kill
sections.purpose: CD4/MHC II signaling and CD8/MHC I killing; distinguish infected cell from extracellular microbe; need activation context.

sections.title: 7. B Cells Become Antibody Factories
sections.purpose: B cell activation, proliferation, plasma cells secreting antibodies and memory formation; explain why binding helps neutralize/opsonize.

sections.title: 8. The Response Resolves, but the Record Remains
sections.purpose: Inflammation subsides, debris clearance, pathogen control, memory cells persist; connect primary response curve to future responses.

sections.title: 9. The Spleen and Thymus Have Different Jobs
sections.purpose: Contrast lymph node filtering lymph, spleen monitoring blood and thymus training T cells; marrow as cell source.

sections.title: 10. One Network, Three Jobs
sections.purpose: Lymph returns via ducts to venous circulation, while intestinal lacteals carry fats; synthesis ties transport, immune protection, and nutrient absorption together.

who-cares.label: Who Cares?
who-cares.targetWords: Three short high-impact summaries plus 350–550-word More Info each
who-cares.style: Digestive-style provocative but defensible title, compact compelling summary, optional More Info containing a mechanism-rich explanation, clear analogies and limitations. No hype or fabricated claims.

entries.title: You have another circulation system, but it has no heart.
entries.hook: Blood capillaries continually deliver fluid to tissues. The lymphatic network collects the excess, passes it through nodes and returns it to veins without a central pump. Valves, vessel contractions, muscle movement, and breathing make that work.
moreInfoConcepts: Initial lymphatic endothelial flaps and anchoring filaments
One-way valves and intrinsic collecting-vessel contraction
Comparison with closed blood vascular circulation
entries.sourceStatus: Directly grounded in source lectures; pump physiology can be externally contextualized.

entries.title: Your thymus protects you partly by rejecting your own immune cells.
entries.hook: T-cell development is not simply a matter of producing more defenders. Developing cells must learn to recognize presented peptides without attacking normal tissue indiscriminately. Many fail this selection process.
moreInfoConcepts: T-cell development in thymic cortex and medulla
Positive and negative selection; central tolerance
How thymic involution changes output with age
entries.sourceStatus: Thymic structure and tolerance are in lectures; selection details are an explicitly labeled scientific extension.

entries.title: Your immune system responds to a familiar threat differently than to a stranger.
entries.hook: The first encounter with an antigen can take time to organize. After memory B and T cells form, a later encounter can produce a much faster and larger response. That is the fundamental logic underlying vaccination.
moreInfoConcepts: Memory B-cell and memory T-cell formation
IgM/IgG titer curves as lecture examples
Vaccination as an external contextual application; note variation by pathogen
entries.sourceStatus: Primary/secondary response grounded in lecture; vaccination explanation is contextual extension.

scientificReviewQueue.issue: Guide asks what hormone stimulates B-cell differentiation and what happens in its absence; supplied slides identify thymosins with T-cell maturation, not a binary B-cell hormone rule.
scientificReviewQueue.handling: Do not invent a course answer. Explain bone marrow B-cell and thymus T-cell differentiation as supported; request instructor clarification before turning ambiguous wording into a graded flashcard.
scientificReviewQueue.outsideBasis: Janeway/NCBI immunobiology: B lineage develops in marrow, T lineage matures in thymus; IL-7 supports B development in marrow niches.

scientificReviewQueue.issue: Course groups lymph nodes, thymus, spleen as three encapsulated organs, while broader immunology also describes bone marrow as a primary lymphoid organ and tonsils/MALT as organized lymphoid structures.
scientificReviewQueue.handling: State course answer prominently, then explain classification conventions without contradicting the instructor silently.

scientificReviewQueue.topic: Lymph node flow through B and T cell zones
scientificReviewQueue.issue: Lecture shorthand depicts lymph flowing through B cells then T cells as consecutive objects. The physical route is via subcapsular, trabecular and medullary sinuses, with immune cells housed in adjoining compartments.
scientificReviewQueue.handling: Teach both the course sequence of regions and the actual sinus pathway; clarify lymphocyte traffic versus fluid movement.

scientificReviewQueue.issue: Normal nucleated cells express MHC I. It presents cellular peptides; infected/abnormal peptide display plus proper T-cell recognition can lead to cytotoxic attack.
scientificReviewQueue.handling: Avoid stating that MHC I itself appears only on infected cells.

scientificReviewQueue.issue: Class II MHC presentation activates antigen-specific helper T cells, which can help B cells; antibody production is not an automatic direct consequence of every MHC II display.
scientificReviewQueue.handling: Show the intervening helper-T, B-cell, plasma-cell steps.

scientificReviewQueue.issue: An early T-cell slide uses “defensins” for cytotoxic release, whereas later cytotoxic/NK slides show perforin and apoptosis; the mechanistic distinction matters.
scientificReviewQueue.handling: Use perforin/granzymes and death-receptor pathways where appropriate; identify lecture wording without making a false equivalence.

scientificReviewQueue.issue: Overlapping entry flaps produce net one-way entry of fluid/cells, but the lecture claim that pathogens cannot leave vessels anywhere is too absolute.
scientificReviewQueue.handling: Explain normal valve function; do not claim the lymphatic system prevents all downstream dissemination.

scientificReviewQueue.topic: Innate, adaptive, active and passive categories
scientificReviewQueue.issue: The immunity diagram places innate and acquired under specific resistance, which risks conflating innate immunity with antigen-specific adaptive immunity.
scientificReviewQueue.handling: Use a clear two-axis comparison: innate vs adaptive; natural/artificial active vs passive within acquired/adaptive immunity.

scientificReviewQueue.topic: Lymphocyte life spans, fractions, lymph-node removal efficiency and fever threshold
scientificReviewQueue.issue: Slides list four-year lymphocyte lifespan, 80% T cells, 99% antigen capture, and fever above 37.2°C; these vary by cell, context, measurement and definition.
scientificReviewQueue.handling: Retain course numbers as reported slide values if relevant for a test, but distinguish them from universal physiological laws.

scientificReviewQueue.issue: The phrase that an ordinary cold will kill anyone infected with HIV is not generally correct. Autoimmunity is not exclusively antibody-based.
scientificReviewQueue.handling: Explain HIV preferentially damages CD4+ T-cell function and that advanced untreated disease can cause opportunistic infections; describe autoimmunity as misdirected T-cell and/or antibody responses.

scientificReviewQueue.issue: The slide says “dolar”; classical Latin term is “dolor”. Four signs listed; some sources add a fifth, loss of function.
scientificReviewQueue.handling: Use four-course-item list with correct spelling and a small note that some texts discuss a fifth.

scientificReviewQueue.issue: Anatomy deck describes five tonsils, including two lingual tonsils, but lingual lymphoid tissue is often a collection of multiple nodules rather than two discrete uniform organs.
scientificReviewQueue.handling: Teach named positions, Waldeyer’s ring and course-labeled five regions; avoid generalizing as a universal count.

authoringRules: Preserve course terms, its three encapsulated organs and exact seven nonspecific defenses explicitly; clearly distinguish valid scientific additions and clarification notes.

General Overview is genuinely brief and accessible; Deep Dive is comprehensive and explanatory; How It Connects is a continuous story and avoids repeating a glossary; Who Cares? has three surprising mechanism-rich essays; Exam Cram is concise and instructor aligned.
No article or practice question is claimed to be written or validated in Stage 1. Deliver these in subsequent stages.
Give each future article section a stable unique ID and source slideRefs by slide number; preserve canonical text for Notes anchoring.
Do not turn disputed course statements into unqualified graded answers before review.
Maintain separately authored concept bank and practice bank, with per-subject IDs, linked source section references, and reusable UI.
Do not claim that microscopic immune cells are directly visualizable in the gross BodyParts3D model; perform a representation audit for Stage 5.
Gallery later: deduplicate slide figures, preserve original names/slide numbers and credits and extract WebP for practical inspection.
